entries.e5af2d8b0924e5fb321a1f2679f4a0bf743948e3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.5.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.5.22" sID="gen124252" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> <hi type="italic">But the fruit</hi> <note n="93"> <div sID="gen124254" type="x-p"/> “In the service of <hi type="italic">sin</hi> the toil is so great that, in comparison thereof, the benefit is as nothing; in the service of <hi type="italic">God</hi> the benefit is so great that, in comparison thereof, the labour is as nothing. Where the flesh rules all, the ‘work’ exceeds the ‘fruit;’ and therefore, without even mentioning the ‘work,’ it is called the ‘fruit’ of the Spirit. (See <reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.9 Bible:Eph.5.11">Ephesians 5:9, 11</reference>.)” — Bishop Sanderson.<div eID="gen124254" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic"> of the Spirit</hi>. In the former part of the description he condemned the whole nature of man as producing nothing but evil and worthless fruits. He now informs us that all virtues, all proper and well regulated affections, proceed from the Spirit, that is, from the grace of God, and the renewed nature which we derive from Christ. As if he had said, “Nothing but what is evil comes from man; nothing good comes but from the Holy Spirit.” There have often appeared in unrenewed men remarkable instances of gentleness, integrity, temperance, and generosity; but it is certain that all were but specious disguises. Curius and Fabrieius were distinguished for courage, Cato for temperance, Scipio for kindness and generosity, Fabius for patience; but it was only in the sight of men, and as members of civil society, that they were so distinguished. In the sight of God nothing is pure but what proceeds from the fountain of all purity.<div eID="gen124253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124255" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Joy</hi> does not here, I think, denote that “joy in the Holy Ghost” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.14.17">Romans 14:17</reference>,) of which he speaks elsewhere, but that cheerful behavior towards our fellow-men which is the opposite of moroseness.<hi type="italic"> Faith</hi> means truth, and is contrasted with cunning, deceit, and falsehood, as <hi type="italic">peace</hi> is with quarrels and contentions. <hi type="italic">Long-suffering</hi> is gentleness of mind, which disposes us to take everything in good part, and not to be easily offended. The other terms require no explanation, for the dispositions of the mind must be learned from the outward conduct.<div eID="gen124255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124256" type="x-p"/>But if spiritual men are known by their works, what judgment, it will be asked, shall we form of wicked men and idolaters, who exhibited an illustrious resemblance of all the virtues? for it is evident from their works that they were spiritual. I reply, as all the works of the flesh do not appear openly in a carnal man, but his carnaltry is discovered by one or another vice, so a single virtue will not entitle us to conclude that a man is spiritual. Sometimes it will be made evident, by other vices, that sin reigns in him; and this observation may be easily applied to all the cases which I have enumerated.<div eID="gen124256" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.5.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124252" osisID="Gal.5.22" type="section"/>
entries.ac2ce9f163082a95b69e1811a923cac6388b5034: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.5.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.5.23" sID="gen124257" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi> <hi type="italic">Against such there is no law</hi>. Some understand these words as meaning simply that the law is not directed against good works, “from evil manners have sprung good laws.” But Paul’s real meaning is deeper and less obvious; namely, that, where the Spirit reigns, the law has no longer any dominion. By moulding our hearts to his own righteousness, the Lord delivers us from the severity of the law, so that our intercourse with himself is not regulated by its covenant, nor our consciences bound by its sentence of condemnation. Yet the law continues to teach and exhort, and thus performs its own office; but our subjection to it is withdrawn by the Spirit of adoption. He thus ridicules the false apostles, who, while they enforced subjection to the law, were not less eager to release themselves from its yoke. The only way, he tells us, in which this is accomplished, is, when the Spirit of God obtains dominion, from which we are led to conclude that they had no proper regard to spiritual righteousness.<div eID="gen124258" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.5.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124257" osisID="Gal.5.23" type="section"/>
entries.abcc568b7d65594befb0bb87548c2c801486f120: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.5.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.5.24" sID="gen124259" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> <hi type="italic">And they that are Christ’s</hi>. He adds this, in order to show that all Christians have renounced the flesh, and therefore enjoy freedom. While he makes this statement, the apostle reminds the Galatians what true Christianity is, so far as relates to the life, and thus guards them against a false profession of Christianity. The word <hi type="italic">crucified</hi> is employed to point out that the mortification of the flesh is the effect of the cross of Christ. This work does not belong to man. By the grace of Christ<div eID="gen124260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124261" type="x-p"/>“we have been planted together in the likeness of his death” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.5">Romans 6:5</reference>,)<div eID="gen124261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124262" type="x-p"/>that we no longer might live unto ourselves. If we are buried with Christ, by true self-denial, and by the destruction of the old man, we shall then enjoy the privilege of the sons of God. The flesh is not yet indeed entirely destroyed; but it has no right to exercise dominion, and ought to yield to the Spirit. The <hi type="italic">flesh</hi> and its<hi type="italic"> lusts</hi> are a figure of speech of exactly the same import with the <hi type="italic">tree</hi> and its <hi type="italic">fruits</hi>. The <hi type="italic">flesh</hi> itself is the depravity of corrupt nature, from which all evil actions proceed. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.15.19">Matthew 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.7.21">Mark 7:21</reference>.) Hence it follows, that the members of Christ have cause to complain, if they are still held to be in bondage to the law, from which all who have been regenerated by his Spirit are set free.<div eID="gen124262" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.5.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124259" osisID="Gal.5.24" type="section"/>
entries.c015ccaf72b67b721b3c2d4db9e9777eccb8ae06: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.5.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.5.25" sID="gen124263" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> <hi type="italic">If we live in the Spirit.</hi> According to his usual custom, the apostle draws from the doctrine a practical exhortation. The death of the flesh is the life of the Spirit. If the Spirit of God lives in us, let him govern our actions. There will always be many persons daring enough to make a false boast of living in the Spirit, but the apostle challenges them to a proof of the fact. As the soul does not remain idle in the body, but gives motion and rigour to every member and part, so the Spirit of God cannot dwell in us without manifesting himself by the outward effects. By the <hi type="italic">life</hi> is here meant the inward power, and by the <hi type="italic">walk</hi> the outward actions. The metaphorical use of the word <hi type="italic">walk</hi>, which frequently occurs, describes works as evidences of the spiritual life.<div eID="gen124264" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.5.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124263" osisID="Gal.5.25" type="section"/>

26. Let us not be desirous of vain-glory, The special exhortations which were addressed to the Galatians were not more necessary for them than they are adapted to our own time. Of many evils existing in society at large, and particularly in the church, ambition is the mother. Paul therefore directs us to guard against it, for the vain-glory (κενοδοξία) of which he speaks is nothing else than ambition, (filimia,) or the desire of honor, by which every one desires to excel all others. The heathen philosophers do not condemn every desire of glory; but among Christians, whoever is desirous of glory departs from true glory, and therefore is justly charged with idle and foolish ambition. It is not lawful for us to glow but in God alone. Every other kind of glorying is pure vanity. Mutual provocations and envyings are the daughters of ambition. He who aspires to the highest rank must of necessity envy all others, and disrespectful, biting, stinging language is the unavoidable consequence.

                     </ns0:gap>. 1.3.</ns0:note> faith which worketh by love <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">And that is, by believing in Christ Jesus, which Faith is not an idle, inactive inoperative Faith; but such a Faith <ns0:hi>as worketh by love,</ns0:hi> both towards God and to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards men in an obedience to all the commandments of God: yet is not the Soul justified, nor shall it stand righteous before God in and for this obedience, which neither is Faith, nor goeth before it, but followeth it, as the true, proper, and ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary effect of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note> Ye did run well <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">This was once your Faith, your profession, and according to this you directed the course of your Life and Actions; who hath hindred you in your course, or turned you out of your way, or given you a check in your race.</ns0:note>, who did <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 3.1.</ns0:note>

                  </ns0:note> hinder you that you should not obey the truth <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And hath made you disobedient to, or to swerve from the truth which you for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />merly owned and professed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 This perswasion <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">This new opinion into which Seducers have misled you, which, by imbracing it, you have made yours;</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>cometh</ns0:hi> not of him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 1.6<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> that calleth you <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Is not <ns0:hi>from God,</ns0:hi> who hath <ns0:hi>called you</ns0:hi> out of darkness into marvellous light, unto fellowship with himself, into a state of Grace and Favour with him, and to the hopes of Eternal Life; and who yet calleth you by his Gospel: It must therefore be from the Devil and his Instruments, who go about to seduce and per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vert you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This is a proverbial expression, which (as others of that nature) is applicable in more cases than one. The Apostle made use of it, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.6. to perswade that Church to purge their Communion, by casting out the incestuous person: he maketh use of it here to perswade them to take heed of ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitting any principles of false Doctrine, which he compareth to <ns0:hi>leaven,</ns0:hi> (as our Saviour does, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 16.6, 12.) And that very fitly, both in regard of the sowre, and of the diffusive na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture of it; the latter of which is here chiefly intended. The truths of God having such dependance one upon another, that he who erreth in any one Doctrine of Faith, seldom continu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth long sound as to other points.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 2.3. & 8.22.</ns0:note> I have confidence in you through the Lord, that you will be none otherwise minded <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Apostle (according to his usual method) sweetneth his sharp reproof of this Church for their deviations from the Faith of the Gospel, with a declaration of his good opinion of them; declaring that he had a confidence in them, that through the Grace of God they would be reduced to the truth, or kept from wandring from it, and that in matters of Faith they would be all of the same mind.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 1.7.</ns0:note> he that troubleth you shall bear <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, whosoever he be <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And for those who endea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />voured to seduce and pervert them,</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">God should reward them according to their works. He seems to aim at some par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticular false Teacher, (whose Name he concealeth,) who gave this Church this trouble.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 And I brethren, if I yet preach circumci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">It should seem by what the Apostle saith in this verse, that some of these false Teachers had quoted the Apostle for them, as if he himself had preached circumcision; possibly taking ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vantage from his circumcising <ns0:hi>Timothy,</ns0:hi> not distinguishing be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />twixt what was done by <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> as of liberty, and to avoid the offence of the Jews, and what they pressed as necessary to be done, (besides believing in Christ) for Justification, Now (saith the Apostle) if I yet preach up circumcision as necessary to be observed,</ns0:note>, why do I yet suffer persecution <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Why am I then persecuted by the Jews, as one apostatized from their Religion?</ns0:note>? then is the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 1.23<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> offence of the cross ceased <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>cross,</ns0:hi> he either means <ns0:hi>the cross of Christ</ns0:hi>; then the sence is, it is my opposing the observance of their law, that more offendeth them than my preaching of Christ crucified. Or else, he meaneth, <ns0:hi>the a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>licti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons</ns0:hi> which he suffered for the sake of Christ and the Gospel; (in which sense the term is used, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 16.24. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 9.23. and 14.27.) Then the sense is, that all sufferings for the own<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing and preaching of Christ are at end; let us but yield the Jews that point (that Christians are obliged to the observance of the law of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi>) the great quarrel between them and us is at end; but their dayly persecuting of me is a sufficient demon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stration that I do not preach up circumcision.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:482" />12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 7.25. 1 Cor. 5.13.</ns0:note> I would they were even cut off that trouble you.<ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">I wish that God would some way or other put an end to these that trouble you, This <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> speaketh not out of hatred to their persons, but out of a zeal to the Glory of God, and a just indignation against these men, who had so much hindred the salvation of the Members of this Church. And it is not impro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable that the Apostle here spake by the Spirit of prophecy; as knowing God would cut them off, so that his, and the like im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />precations of holy men in Scripture are not to be drawn into presidents, or made matters for our imitation, unless we had the same discerning of Spirits which they had, or the same Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit of Prophecy and Revelations from God as to future things. But how far it is lawful or unlawful for ordinary persons, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Ministers, or private Christians to pray against Gods, or his Churches Enemies, is a question for the arguing which, this place is too narrow.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">A <ns0:hi>liberty</ns0:hi> from the covenant of the Law; and the curse of the Law, as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 3.13. From servile fear, as <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 1.74. and from sin, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.7.</ns0:note>, only <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 8.9. 1 Pet. 2.16. 2 Pet. 2.19. Jude 4.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>use</ns0:hi> not liberty for an occasi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on to the flesh <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">But you must take heed, that you do not abuse this liberty by making it an <ns0:hi>occasion for sin</ns0:hi>; so as from thence to conclude, that you may give your flesh more liberty in obeying the lusts of it: you must not think, that the Gospel hath set you at liberty from the obedience of the Law; the Gospel liberty to which you are called doth not set you free from the duty of love, either to God or men.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 9.19. chap. 6.2.</ns0:note> by love serve one ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">There<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore by <ns0:hi>love serve one another.</ns0:hi> Our Christian liberty neither freeth us from the serving of God, nor from our mutual serving each other to love. According to <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.8. <ns0:hi>Owe nothing to any man, but this, that you love one another.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 7.12. Jam. 2.8.</ns0:note> all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Levit. 19.18. Mat. 22.37, 39.</ns0:note> Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thy self <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The whole Will of God, containing our duty towards men, is reducible to this one thing, <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi>; for whatsoever God hath commanded us to do towards men, is but a branch from this root, and must flow from Love as its principle. Or the whole will of God concerning man is fulfilled in this one thing of love; where love to God is not excluded, but supposed, as the root of our love to our Neighbour; for our Neighbour is to be loved for God. Thus <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.8. <ns0:hi>He that loveth another, hath fulfilled the Law</ns0:hi>: And 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4.20. the Apostle proveth, that a man cannot love God unless he loveth his Brother; and 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.5. <ns0:hi>The end of the Commandment is charity</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Yet what the Papists would conclude from hence, (<ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> that it is possible for a man to fulfil the Law, because it is possible for him to love his Neighbour;) doth by no means follow; for the Apostle 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.5. telleth us, This love must proceed <ns0:hi>out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and faith unfeigned.</ns0:hi> Mr. <ns0:hi>Calvin</ns0:hi> observeth well, that the Apostle here mentioneth <ns0:hi>love to men</ns0:hi> as the ful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />filling of the Law, in opposition to the false Teachers; who made the <ns0:hi>fulfilling of the Law</ns0:hi> to lye in the observance of the ceremonies of the law, whereas the great thing which the law of God requireth is <ns0:hi>love,</ns0:hi> out of a <ns0:hi>pure heart, good conscience,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>faith unfeigned.</ns0:hi> So that he who believeth with a Faith un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feigned, and out of that principle, with a pure heart, and a good conscience, loveth his Neighbour as himself, shall be by God accounted to have fulfilled the law; for <ns0:hi>love is the end of the law.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 But if ye bite, and devour one another <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This lets us know, that there were great contentions and divisions amongst the members of this Church, whether (which is probable) occasioned by their differences in and about the Doctrine of <ns0:hi>Iustification,</ns0:hi> or upon other accounts we are not told, but upon whatever account they were raised, they were contrary to that serving one another in love, to which the Apostle had exhorted them. Nor did they terminate in a meer dislike of, and displicency to each other, but break out into overt acts, more becoming dogs than christians, and therefore 'tis expressed under the notion of <ns0:hi>biting</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>devouring.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, take heed ye be not consumed one of ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The issue of which the Apostle prophesieth, would be a <ns0:hi>consuming</ns0:hi> one another; they being actions that had a natural tendency to this end.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:hi>This</ns0:hi> I say then, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 13 1 Pet. 2.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> walk in the spirit <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Apostle having <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 13. cautioned them against <ns0:hi>turn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the grace of God into wantonness,</ns0:hi> by using their <ns0:hi>liberty as an occasion to the flesh</ns0:hi>; here he directeth them to the best means for the avoiding thereof, <ns0:hi>viz. walking in the Spirit.</ns0:hi> Where by <ns0:hi>Spirit</ns0:hi> he doth not mean our own <ns0:hi>Spirits,</ns0:hi> or the guide and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duct of our own reason; for the term <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> set (as here) in opposition to the <ns0:hi>flesh,</ns0:hi> is in no place of Scripture understood of any other than the holy Spirit of God, which dwelleth in, and influenceth Believers, guiding them both by a rule from without (which is the word of God, given by its inspiration,) and by its inward motions and operations. <ns0:hi>Walking,</ns0:hi> signifieth the directing of their whole conversations. The phrase <ns0:hi>in the Spirit,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>after the Spirit, Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.1. seem to be of the same import, unless the alteration of the <ns0:hi>Preposition</ns0:hi> signifieth, that christians are not only to look to the word of God dictated by the Holy Spirit as their rule, and to listen to its dictates, but also to look up to the Holy Spirit for its strength and assistance; and implieth a promise of such assistance. The sense is, let your whole con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versation be according to the external rule of the Gospel, and the more inward motions, directions, and inclinations of the Spirit of Christ; dwelling and working in you, and moving you to the obedience of that word.</ns0:note>, and ye <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> shall not fulfil the lusts of the flesh <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This doing, though the flesh be yet in you, and you will find the lustings and warn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings of it, yet you shall not <ns0:hi>fulfil</ns0:hi> the sinful desires and lustings of it, that is, sin, though it be in you, shall not be in domini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on in you; it shall not reign in your mortal bodies, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.12. <ns0:hi>Let not sin reign in your mortal bodies, that you should obey it in the lusts thereof.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 7.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>, in our mind and rational part also; <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.21. And some of the <ns0:hi>fruits of the flesh,</ns0:hi> which are af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terward mention'd, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 19.20. (such as <ns0:hi>Idolatry, Heresies,</ns0:hi> &c.) cannot be referred to the sensitive part. But by these terms are either to be understood the unregenerate part of man; or rather, that carnal concupiscence which we derived from <ns0:hi>Adam,</ns0:hi> and is seated in our rational as well as sensitive appetite; which opposeth it self to the divine rule, and to the dictates and motions of the Spirit of God.</ns0:note> lusteth against the spirit <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This concupiscence moveth strongly against the directions of the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit.</ns0:note>, and the spirit against the flesh <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">And the Holy Spirit of God dwelling in the Saints, mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veth as potently against the propensions and inclinations of the flesh.</ns0:note>, and these are contrary the one to the other <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">For they are two contrary principles, and work con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trarily in their motions and inclinations.</ns0:note>, so <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 7.19.</ns0:note> that ye cannot do the things that ye would <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">So that even the best of Gods people cannot at all times do either what they should do, (according to the precept of the word,) or what they would do, according to the bent of their regenerate part.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 6 & 8.2.</ns0:note> if ye be led by the spirit, ye are, not under the law <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>To be led by the Spirit,</ns0:hi> and to <ns0:hi>walk in the Spirit,</ns0:hi> are the same thing; and differ only as the cause and the effect. To be <ns0:hi>un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the law,</ns0:hi> is to be under the <ns0:hi>curse</ns0:hi> of it, or <ns0:hi>coaction</ns0:hi> of it, and an obligation to the performance of the ceremonial Law. The reason is, because the Spirit is a Spirit of Adoption and liber<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty; and where it is, it teacheth to serve the Lord without fear from a principle of freedom and ingenuity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note>, witchcraft <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The product of compacts with the Devil; by vertue of which, the persons so contracting are assisted by the power of evil Spirits to produce effects besides the ordinary course and order of Nature, and for the most part mischievous to others.</ns0:note>, hatred <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">And not these gross crimes only are the fruits of the flesh, but also <ns0:hi>abiding hatred</ns0:hi> of our brethren in our hearts, enmities to others, (as the word signifieth.)</ns0:note>, vari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The result of which, are <ns0:hi>variances,</ns0:hi> mens quarrellings, and contendings one with another for little or no cause.</ns0:note>, emulations <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
